    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that hilton is making a big play in South Florida with its Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort.
    • Sources indicate that the resort caters primarily to business and group travelers (it’s attached to a massive events space), but it’s also a strong option for vacationers looking for some R&R.
    • In a recent development, room rates typically run $300 to $600 a night, depending on the season, but you can also use Hilton Honors benefits to make your stay more affordable.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that hilton is making a big play in South Florida with its Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort. The massive 1,000-room property — which underwent an $80 million renovation before opening under the Signia Hilton brand in May 2026 — sits on the beach in Hollywood, Florida, just outside of Fort Lauderdale.

    Sources indicate that the resort caters primarily to business and group travelers (it’s attached to a massive events space), but it’s also a strong option for vacationers looking for some R&R. The main downside: The location isn’t great if your trip primarily revolves around off-property excursions, dining and nightlife.

    In a recent development, room rates typically run $300 to $600 a night, depending on the season, but you can also use Hilton Honors benefits to make your stay more affordable. There’s also a resort fee of $59 per night — but Hilton waives that when you book using Hilton points.

    Hilton covered the cost of my stay for two nights, but the opinions in this review are my own. Here’s what guests can expect at this oceanfront resort.

    Since the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort is part of Hilton Honors, there are several ways to book a stay there.

    Sources indicate that if you’re using Hilton points, expect to pay 70,000 to 80,000 points a night when standard rooms are available. Hilton elite status — a benefit you can earn by holding any Hilton Honors credit card — gets you the fifth-night-free perk, where you stay for at least five nights but pay for four when booking with points.

    For example, if you were to stay five nights at 80,000 points a night, you’d pay 320,000 points total, bringing down your average nightly rate to 64,000 points.

    In a recent development, you can also book using Hilton’s generous free night certificates, which can be used at almost any property in the portfolio. If you hold the Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card, you automatically get a certificate each year. It’s also possible to earn certificates through reaching spending thresholds on the card and on the Hilton Honors American Express Surpass® Card. Terms apply.

    It has been revealed that make sure to check the cash rate against the points rate to make sure you’re getting good value from your redemption. NerdWallet values Hilton points at 0.4 cent apiece.

    For cash bookings of two nights or more, you might consider using The Hotel Collection via American Express’ travel portal for eligible cardholders. Eligible bookings come with benefits like a $100 property credit and other amenities subject to availability, including a room upgrade, early check-in and late checkout.

    Keep in mind that third-party bookings typically don’t earn Hilton points or count toward elite status qualification.

    It’s hard to miss the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort, with its signature H-shaped facade and sleek white-and-glass exterior.

    Recent findings suggest that stepping into the hotel, I was immediately struck by the lush greenery filling the entrance and indoor courtyard. The grand lobby has soaring glass ceilings, giving the space a greenhouse feel, although the strong air conditioning keeps you cool.

    It has been revealed that despite its massive size, it doesn’t have a sprawling layout, which I appreciated. Everything is close together, and you can walk from the check-in counter to any of the indoor restaurants in under a minute.

    In a recent development, I stayed in an oceanfront suite with a balcony, which was spacious and had a fun beachy vibe. To get to the rooms, you’ll need to use either the north or south tower elevator banks.

    In the living room, there was a large sitting area featuring a TV, a couch, an accent chair and a four-person high-top table.

    Although I didn’t spend too much time on the balcony — the October balminess was a bit too much for me — I enjoyed stepping out each morning to admire the view.

    The bedroom had a king bed with extremely comfortable bedding and an oversized chair that was a great spot to relax and read a book by the window.

    The bathroom was spacious, featuring a shower and a separate tub (something every room has).

    Even the standard room I toured felt roomy. I liked that it shared similar elements with the suite, including the oversized lounge chair.

    This is what you’d normally get when booking a room at the cheapest points price.

    There are several dining venues on the property, ranging from a grab-and-go cafe to a high-end steakhouse. It is a luxury resort, so expect the prices to reflect that.

    It has been revealed that for breakfast, you can head to Palmea Kitchen, which is also open for lunch. I had the breakfast buffet, which offered a nice spread of classics, from hot food items and pastries to cold cuts and smoked salmon.

    If you don’t have time for a sit-down breakfast, you can head next door to The Press, which offers made-to-order and grab-and-go food options throughout the day. You can also get smoothies, juices, snacks, pastries and other sweet treats.

    The Canteen is another grab-and-go option that also sells snacks, drinks, souvenirs and sundries, similar to a convenience store.

    For lunch and dinner, try Solara. It doesn’t have a traditional restaurant feel, as it’s mostly an indoor-outdoor bar space. One side connects to the lobby, while the other side faces the Solara adults-only pool.

    It serves a lunch menu, as well as a substantial bar food menu that’s available late into the night.

    You can also eat at Playa Beach Bar & Grill, a beachside restaurant serving Latin-inspired cuisine. I enjoyed spending a lazy lunch there and watching the waves crash onto the shore.

    For a fancy sit-down dinner, go to Diplomat Prime, the property’s steakhouse. We had a group dinner at the restaurant, and the meats were, of course, the highlight. But don’t sleep on the seafood, which was also delicious.

    One of the best parts of the Dip, as it’s affectionately known, is its location right on the beach. Guests can access the stretch of beach directly adjacent to the property. But it’s not a private beach, so you might encounter crowds.

    I didn’t spend any time on the beach itself — it was extremely windy while I was there — but the hotel’s resort fee includes amenities like a beach lounge (umbrella not included), a daily one-hour kayak or paddleboard rental, and beachfront yoga classes.

    If you don’t want to get sand everywhere, you can head to one of the three pool options: the adults-only Solara pool, the family-friendly lagoon pool and the Verandah Social Club for those 21 and older (requires paid access).

    The family-friendly lagoon spans the length of the property and runs beneath the Solara pool. It also has its own hot tub.

    I spent an afternoon in a cabana at the Verandah Social Club, which has some smaller plunge pools and a hot tub.

    I appreciated the attentive service from the staff there, who constantly checked on whether guests needed anything.

    If you’re looking for other ways to stay active, head to the two-story fitness center, featuring a variety of equipment like free weights, exercise bikes, a rowing machine and treadmills.

    Next door, you’ll find the spa and wellness center. I had a relaxing massage that incorporated hot stones and aromatherapy.

    The locker rooms come with a sauna and steam room, although I wished there were more amenities like a hot tub and cold plunge.

    One of the resort fee inclusions is complimentary high-intensity interval training workout classes at the gym across the street. I signed up for an early morning class. The instructor was friendly, and it was a great way to start my day.

    Other amenities include a complimentary one-hour e-bike rental each day, as well as a kids’ club with various activities (but drop-off fees apply).

    I had a fantastic stay at this resort, but I’d recommend it for a specific traveler.

    If you’re planning to stay on-property your entire trip, it’s a great option. That’s probably why it’s such a popular convention hotel, since everything you need is easily accessible.

    I loved the hotel’s design, including the jungle-like atmosphere in the lobby, and I found the dining options to be tasty, albeit pricey.

    But if your trip revolves around visiting Miami attractions, you’ll likely want to stay closer to the action.

    • Sources indicate that wall Street's early rally unraveled on Thursday, November 19, as even the largest initial public offering in history proved insufficient to restore investor confidence.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By RJ Fulton – Nov 19, 2026 at 5:45PM EST.

    Sources indicate that wall Street's early rally unraveled on Thursday, November 19, as even the largest initial public offering in history proved insufficient to restore investor confidence. Despite Anthropic's (ANT +17.07%) successful stock market debut, selling pressure intensified throughout the session as concerns surrounding elevated valuations and the prospect of further interest rate hikes continued to weigh on equities.

    The S&P 500 (^GSPC -2.02%) fell 2.00% to 7,177, marking its sixth consecutive session of losses and its longest losing streak since April 2024. The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -2.25%) reversed its early gains, closing 2.23% lower at 23,886, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI -2.19%) plunged more than 1,100 points, falling 2.19% to 49,097.

    Industry observers note that selling pressure extended beyond equities, with December gold futures settling 1.50% lower at $3,685.50, while the 10-year Treasury yield eased to 5.05%. All 11 S&P 500 sectors finished in negative territory, with consumer discretionary leading losses at 2.79%.

    Industry observers note that despite the broader market sell-off, Insmed (INSM +20.58%) surged 20.58% following reports that French pharmaceutical giant Sanofi (SNY -2.25%) is considering acquiring the biotechnology organization. Palo Alto Networks (PANW +6.42%) was the S&P 500's best-performing stock, gaining 6.42% after reporting strong quarterly results and raising its fiscal 2027 outlook.

    According to recent reports, conversely, Williams-Sonoma (WSM -15.16%) was the S&P 500's worst-performing stock, plunging 15.16% following its quarterly earnings report. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -7.72%) fell 7.72% following a report from investigative outlet Hunterbrook alleging ties to a blacklisted Chinese server manufacturer.

    Recent findings suggest that anthropic's record-breaking IPO demonstrates that investor appetite for artificial intelligence (AI) remains substantial, even as concerns surrounding technology valuations intensify. However, the sheer size of Anthropic's offering also raises questions about how much capital remains available to support other AI investments.

    With technology companies competing for financing to fund increasingly expensive infrastructure projects, elevated interest rates could force investors to become more selective about which businesses warrant premium valuations.

    It has been revealed that perhaps more concerning is the deterioration in market breadth over the past week.     #50692. Industry News: AI May Write The Code, But Real Enterprise Value Is In Understanding It

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (974 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: AI May Write The Code, But Real Enterprise Value Is In Understanding It

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (974 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Rob Kim, CTO at Presidio, driving innovation and digital transformation through AI, cloud and next-gen infrastructure solutions.
    • According to recent reports, ​We’re watching a dynamic play out with AI at enterprise scale.
    • The following phrase from Notion design engineer Jeffrey Litt has reshaped how I think about both coding and corporate AI strategy.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rob Kim, CTO at Presidio, driving innovation and digital transformation through AI, cloud and next-gen infrastructure solutions.

    According to recent reports, ​We’re watching a dynamic play out with AI at enterprise scale. Organizations that race ahead with AI agent deployments are discovering an uncomfortable truth: velocity without understanding isn’t transformation—it’s accumulation (AI slop). Every AI workflow shipped without a clear mental model of what it does, who owns it or how it evolves adds to a balance sheet nobody is tracking.

    The following phrase from Notion design engineer Jeffrey Litt has reshaped how I think about both coding and corporate AI strategy.

    Sources indicate that “Understanding isn’t a verification step. It’s the substrate for participation.”.

    In a recent development, this reframes the entire AI conversation—both on the keyboard and in the boardroom. Verification is being automated (so stop trying to impede). What can’t be automated is the human capacity to generate new ideas, weigh tradeoffs and steer direction, and that capacity depends entirely on whether we understand the systems we’re building with (namely AI output).

    In IT, we talk about technical debt constantly but rarely talk about cognitive debt—the slow erosion of a team’s mental model as code accumulates faster than our ability to comprehend it.

    According to recent reports, when developers can’t reason about their own systems, they stop being authors and become passengers. It’s the essence of vibe coding; shipping changes that work, but for reasons nobody on the team can articulate. The impact may not show up until several months after the first sprint, with a critical bug that surfaces without anyone knowing where it came from.

    The immediate response is to gate everything behind review—in the form of human approval. That’s a losing strategy in the AI era because agents outproduce human reviewers by exponentially. The more productive (but challenging) response is to redesign how teams learn what their tools have built.

    For decades, the default model of human participation in software has been approval:.

    • A change advisory board convenes.

    This worked when humans wrote every line of code, because the approver generally understood what they were approving.

    It has been revealed that in the AI era, that assumption breaks. Approving output you cannot evaluate is not governance, but theater. Understanding is the only form of participation that scales: when a team genuinely comprehends what their agents are building, they won’t just “rubber-stamp it,” but instead they reshape it, steer it and teach the system what good looks like.

    The human element doesn’t act as a gate of control (and slow things down) but instead is the force that guides a more accurate output—zeroshot. This approach can be simplified with the following three techniques (at least to start):.

    A traditional PR shows you what changed but a curriculum-style explanation shows you why it changed, what system it lives in and what mental model you need before the diff makes sense.

    Picture a change that converts a 2D top-down game into an isometric view. A flat diff is unreadable. A curriculum-style explainer starts with the rendering engine, then the coordinate system, then a plain-English summary (“we’re faking 3D with 2D drawing tricks”), then an interactive widget where you drag objects around to see the effect—only then the annotated line-by-line change.

    Recent findings suggest that litt built a tool that generates these documents automatically and drops them into his agentic software as collaborative pages. Quizzes at the end of each section force active recall—a technique borrowed straight from educational research. You can’t merge until you pass.

    The unlock is to treat explanations as a first-class artifact, not a comment thread.

    This pattern borrows from Seymour Papert, the MIT researcher who argued decades ago that children learn math best by “living in Mathland.” Now, just replace “Mathland” with the codebase, and you get the concept of microworlds: interactive simulations where developers explore code behavior rather than reading about it.

    Microworlds collapse the gap between reading code and running code. They turn comprehension from a passive activity into an interactive one.

    Most software is built by teams, but most AI-coding workflows are deeply individual.

    • A context window in your head.

    • A PR nobody else can interpret.

    It has been revealed that litt’s team inverted this. AI agents live in shared chat channels, and the explanations live in shared documents. Additionally, the coding assistants are integrated into team workspaces versus living in individual IDEs, resulting in a collective cognitive map where everyone sees the same model of the system. This allows “disagreements” to surface early instead of in production. We have applied this procedurally across our own development teams.

    It has been revealed that this isn’t an AI challenge as the technology already exists. The real challenge is shifting cultural where treating “understanding” as a team deliverable, not a personal one.

    Alan Kay (pioneer of object-oriented programming) succinctly captures this argument:.

    “The computer is a tool to help you do what you want to do, not to tell you what you should do.”.

    According to recent reports, in essence, “level humans up.” AI doesn’t have to erode that, rather, it can scaffold it. Don’t automate away understanding in trade for manual (human) control. The temptation in any productivity revolution is to mistake output for progress—heck, we did it with tokens (remember tokenmaxxing?). We can ship lines of code, merge PRs and close tickets infinitely faster with AI, but none of it matters if the team that built it can’t explain it six months from now.

    ​The teams (and enterprises) that win the next decade will be those who treat AI as a learning partner versus a replacement for thought.

    Cognitive debt compounds, while understanding compounds faster—if you willingly invest in it.

    • Anthropic's share price climbed back above $95...
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By John Bromels – Nov 19, 2026 at 6:12PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

    Industry observers note that as the trading day neared its end, all eyes were on Anthropic (ANT +17.07%)stock. Would the market's newest IPO (not to mention the largest IPO in history) stage a late rally and finish the day above $100/share?

    Industry observers note that at 3:30 p.m., it didn't look promising. A midafternoon rally that brought the stock price to $99.62/share fizzled, sending it tumbling back down below $95/share again. But then, at about 3:45 p.m., just 15 minutes before the closing bell, things started moving.

    Anthropic's share price climbed back above $95... then to $96... and $97...

    But then time ran out. The AI heavyweight's shares finished their IPO day at a closing price of $97.17/share, after opening at $111.50/share.

    Here's what that means for investors who bought $1,000 of the company's IPO shares and for those who waited.

    Industry observers note that although Anthropic revealed its official IPO price of $83/share last night, we didn't know what its market debut price would be. That's because the IPO price only applies to designated IPO shares, which are allocated to specific individuals and institutions before public trading ever begins.

    If demand is high -- which, of course, was the case for the highly anticipated Anthropic debut -- shares will begin trading at a higher price than the IPO price. This is exactly what happened with SpaceX's (SPCX -3.53%)recent IPO, which was priced at $135/share, but debuted on the NASDAQ at $150/share.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/19/26.

    In Anthropic's case, it looks as though that debut price of $111.50/share (a 34.3% premium to its IPO price) might have been a bit too optimistic. Immediately after shares started trading at 11:51 a.m., the price dropped sharply. By noon, it had already tumbled below $106/share. Within the first hour, it fell below $100/share, and stayed there for the rest of the day.

    But although it closed well below its debut market price, it was above its IPO price.

    $1,000 would have bought you about 12 shares of Anthropic stock at the $83 IPO price (you'd've had $4 left over).

    At a closing price of $97.17, you'd have made a one-day profit of $14.17/share, or $170.04 for 12 shares, meaning you'd have $1,170.04 (or, if you bought a fractional share with that last $4, you'd have $1,170.72). That's a 17% gain in one day: not too shabby!

    On the other hand, if you missed out on the IPO, but instead bought $1,000 worth of shares right when they debuted at $111.50/share, you'd have been able to afford about 9 shares (8.97 shares, to be exact).

    At a closing price of $97.17, you'd've lost $14.33/share today, or about $129 in total ($128.54, if you'd bought exactly 8.97 shares).

    So, of your $1,000, you'd have $871.46 remaining, a 14.3% loss.

    Industry observers note that meanwhile, if you'd waited to buy shares on the open market until after 1:00 p.m. today, when the worst of the sell-off was already over, you would have bought at a price somewhere between $92.72/share and $99.62/share, meaning you'd have between a 2.5% loss and a 4.8% gain. That translates to a median gain of 1.15% on your $1,000, giving you $1,011.50.

    That's not much, but on a day when all the major indexes were down more than 2%, it's not a terrible return for a few hours' investment.

    Sources indicate that of course, smart investors don't just calculate their gains after a few hours, or even a few days. Instead, they keep their money invested over the long term, measuring success in years, if not decades.

    Given the lack of public information we have about Anthropic's operations and financials, there's no way to know where its share price will end up in three to five years.

    So, while IPO investors can pat themselves on the back for their early win, they should pay attention to Anthropic's news releases and quarterly earnings reports to get a fuller picture of how their investment is playing out over time.

    #50689. ​Your Pharma Contract Is Approved. But Is It A Competitive Deal?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (803 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    ​Your Pharma Contract Is Approved. But Is It A Competitive Deal?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Nithin Mummaneni is the founder and CEO of Infinity Loop.
    • A 300-page pharmaceutical outsourcing agreement can clear legal, quality, regulatory and technical review without anyone asking whether the price is competitive.
    • Industry observers note that ​Each department reviews the agreement through its own responsibilities.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Nithin Mummaneni is the founder and CEO of Infinity Loop.

    A 300-page pharmaceutical outsourcing agreement can clear legal, quality, regulatory and technical review without anyone asking whether the price is competitive.

    Industry observers note that ​Each department reviews the agreement through its own responsibilities. Legal looks at liability, quality reviews manufacturing obligations, and regulatory and technical teams cover their respective areas. What can get lost is the commercial picture: the rates, annual increases, payment arrangements and scope that determine what the business will actually pay.

    Sources indicate that I spent years as a management consultant running contract negotiations for Fortune 500 companies and private equity portfolios. In pharmaceuticals, I rarely met a team that had benchmarked its payment terms or escalation provisions against comparable agreements. We could provide that analysis, but the cost of the analysis could outweigh potential savings, making it difficult for companies to justify. As a result, procurement teams remain in the dark about whether an agreement is commercially competitive. A contract can be fully approved without anyone knowing whether the tech giant is overpaying or leaving savings on the table.

    The most expensive parts of a pharmaceuticals contract are usually the change-control clauses.

    According to recent reports, ​The FDA recommends keeping quality agreements separate from the commercial contract, or structured so they can be separated. This keeps manufacturing responsibilities from getting tangled up with pricing, delivery and liability limits. That makes sense for compliance. It also means a quality team can approve a document that affects costs without anyone in the room reviewing the pricing implications.

    ​Before signing, procurement should understand which required activities are included in the quoted price, what triggers additional charges and how a change affects delivery dates and payments. Quality requirements and change-control obligations both affect what ends up on the invoice, whether or not the teams reviewing them consider that cost.

    Timing matters, too. When scientists or operations teams select the supplier and set the scope first, procurement often joins after the decisions that shape the deal have already been made. By the time the contract reaches procurement, the team is left trying to improve pricing on a deal it had little opportunity to influence.

    ​This often happens with incumbent suppliers. There is value in staying with a provider that has already been qualified, and few pharmaceutical companies want to take on continuity risk unless they have to. Suppliers understand that and often price accordingly.

    ​A proven contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO) can earn a premium. Procurement’s job is to understand how much of that premium reflects the provider’s capability and how much reflects the difficulty of switching.

    Even when switching is off the table, there is still room to negotiate payment arrangements, annual increases, scope and change orders. Understanding those constraints helps procurement decide what to ask for and how to approach the conversation.

    Recent findings suggest that organizations keep outsourcing more. The average organization now works with 286 third-party vendors, up 21% year over year, according to Whistic’s 2025 third-party risk management report.

    Recent findings suggest that ​Lonza’s 2025 annual report describes continued outsourcing in biologics as demand grows and more molecules move toward commercialization. Each new relationship adds contracts, amendments and a performance history that someone needs to understand before the next renewal. Those records often sit across different functions and systems.

    Sources indicate that ​Procurement managers preparing for a renewal may have the signed contract and little else. To understand what the supplier actually delivered or what has changed in the new proposal, they have to request information from other teams and compare documents manually.

    ​That work is slow and expensive. If the evidence only comes together after the renewal has been signed, it is too late to use it to shape that negotiation.

    Sources indicate that at one global biopharmaceutical manufacturer, my company analyzed $350.3 million in spend across its network of outsourced research and development providers. We identified $24.6 million in actionable savings, about 7% of spend. We found those opportunities by bringing contract, supplier and market data together, giving procurement a clearer picture of where it had leverage, what to ask for and how to approach the negotiation.

    ​Paying more for a proven partner may make sense. But the team should understand the rates it is paying and how they compare to the market before making that decision. It should be a deliberate choice.

    It has been revealed that before the next agreement is signed, settle three things: who owns the price review, when it happens and what evidence it needs. Then bring procurement in early enough to act on what it finds. The review matters most when there’s still time to change the deal.​.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 10 stocks we like better than VanEck ETF Trust - VanEck Semiconductor ETF ›.
    • Industry observers note that the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH -2.62%) closed on Nov.
    • With around six weeks left in the year, the chip fund is ahead by about 21 percentage points.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Daniel Sparks – Nov 19, 2026 at 6:23PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than VanEck ETF Trust - VanEck Semiconductor ETF ›.

    Industry observers note that the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH -2.62%) closed on Nov. 17 at $460.10, putting it up around 28% in 2026. The S&P 500 (^GSPC -2.02%) rose about 7% during the same stretch.

    With around six weeks left in the year, the chip fund is ahead by about 21 percentage points. If its lead holds through Dec. 31, it'll have beaten the index for a fourth straight calendar year, after winning in all of the last three. It's never strung together four in a row.

    Industry observers note that the last time it won three straight, the next year went badly. The fund dropped around 34% in 2022, while the S&P 500 lost about 19%.

    According to recent reports, I checked this using year-end closing prices from Yahoo Finance, with dividends left out throughout. That record begins in June 2000. Today's fund only dates to December 2011, though, when VanEck replaced the Semiconductor HOLDRS trust that had traded under the same ticker.

    Either way, the fund's longest run of wins against the S&P 500 is three years. And including dividends doesn't change which years it won.

    In a recent development, the two three-year runs look a lot alike. From the end of 2018 through 2021, the fund gained around 254%, versus about 90% for the index. From the end of 2022 through 2025, it climbed by about 255%, compared with about 78%.

    Of course, what matters to a buyer is what came next. Every winning run in the data (six in all, including single-year wins in 2003 and 2005) was followed by a year when the fund's price fell. The declines ranged from below 3% in 2015 to the 34% drop in 2022.

    And the industry's sales didn't give much warning. Worldwide chip sales hit a record $574.1 billion in 2022, up 3.3% over 2021, according to the Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA). The slowdown came only in the second half, while the fund had been declining since its Dec. 27, 2021, record close.

    Recent findings suggest that then sales dropped 8.2% in 2023 -- the same year the fund gained around 72%. In other words, the stocks moved before the yearly sales numbers did, in both directions.

    I think the main difference between 2026 and 2021 is the starting price. The fund finished 2021 only about 2% below its record close, so investors buying at the start of 2022 paid near-peak prices.

    Sources indicate that this year, the drop came early. The fund's record close was on June 22 at $668.91, up around 86% for the year. It's since lost most of that gain and is about 31% under the record.

    Industry observers note that even so, it hasn't ended a single trading day in 2026 behind the S&P 500 on a year-to-date basis. A winning calendar year, in other words, can still hide a fall of around 31%, and the streak says nothing about the price an investor pays.

    What's kept the fund ahead is spending on artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.

    According to recent reports, showing how strong that spending still is, Nvidia (NVDA -3.30%), the fund's largest holding, posted fiscal third-quarter revenue (the period ended Oct. 25, 2026) of $115.8 billion after the close on Nov. 17, up 103% year over year. Its data center revenue climbed 110% to $107.6 billion, a small slowdown from 117% growth in fiscal Q2. But total revenue grew 20% from the previous quarter, slightly faster than the 18% sequential growth Nvidia posted in fiscal Q2. And management guided for about $130 billion in fiscal fourth-quarter revenue, a period that has an extra week.

    It has been revealed that these were also Nvidia's first results since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO. CFO Colette Kress is filling in as interim CEO. The fund climbed around 4% in after-hours trading that evening.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/19/26.

    Sources indicate that much of the result may hinge on a few stocks. As of Nov. 16, Nvidia accounted for around 17% of the fund's assets, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing accounted for about 10%. Its 10 largest holdings, out of 25, accounted for about 69%.

    According to recent reports, A fourth straight win would be a first for the fund. But the record suggests a streak tells a buyer little about the year after, and the sales numbers gave little warning before the last one ended.

    Recent findings suggest that what a buyer gets now is a price around 31% under the fund's June 22 record close, in a group whose largest member just more than doubled its quarterly revenue. I think the fund is worth considering here, maybe added gradually over the next few months. I'd just size any position with a year like 2022 in mind.

    #50682. Tech Report: Beyond Detecting Fakes: Assuring Identity And Verifying Authorization

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1064 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Beyond Detecting Fakes: Assuring Identity And Verifying Authorization

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Krishnaveni Palanivelu, SVP Cybersecurity Architect, Financial Services.
    • ​Imagine a bank’s fraud team reviewing two incidents.
    • It has been revealed that both involved convincing fakes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Krishnaveni Palanivelu, SVP Cybersecurity Architect, Financial Services.

    ​Imagine a bank’s fraud team reviewing two incidents. In the first, an applicant cleared onboarding using a synthetic identity assembled from stolen personal details and fabricated supporting documents. In the second, a finance employee released a payment after hearing an AI-cloned version of a familiar executive’s voice. The executive never requested it.

    It has been revealed that both involved convincing fakes. But they exposed different failures: accepting an identity that did not represent a real applicant and accepting instructions that did not come from the person supposedly giving them. Stronger onboarding addresses the first. It cannot, by itself, prevent the second.

    Generative AI reduces the time, effort and expertise required to create believable documents, faces, voices and messages. The FBI has warned that criminals use these capabilities to expand fraud and make their approaches more convincing. The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network has also reported suspicious activity involving fraudulent identity documents used to bypass verification.

    It has been revealed that attackers can vary their material, repeat attempts and exploit whichever channel offers the weakest challenge. Training employees to notice an unnatural pause or a distorted image may help today, but it is a fragile foundation for tomorrow’s payment controls.

    Recent findings suggest that detection still matters. However, making it the deciding control leaves the organization dependent on recognizing the next forgery before accepting it. Leaders should ask: What independent evidence must exist before we establish a relationship or allow a consequential action?

    Identity assurance establishes confidence that someone is who they claim to be. It connects the applicant, supporting evidence and subsequent credentials to a real identity. The next checks concern authorization and intent: Is this person permitted to act, and what evidence highlights they knowingly approved this specific request?

    It has been revealed that A customer can authenticate successfully and still be manipulated into paying a criminal. An employee can recognize a voice and mistake familiarity for permission. Authentication establishes control of a credential, but it does not establish informed intent.

    In my article on non-human identity, I argued for attributable actions, defined permissions and accountable ownership across machines and agents. The same discipline must govern human interactions: establish who is acting, preserve that identity through the workflow and verify authority at the point of consequence.

    In banking, account opening and authorized-push-payment fraud require different interventions. Onboarding should corroborate identity evidence against trustworthy sources and examine whether the applicant, device and submitted material belong together. A payment from an established customer requires transaction context: a fresh beneficiary, an unusual amount or signs that someone is directing the customer through the process. Another login challenge may add little protection against persuasion.

    In healthcare, identity assurance can help prevent an impostor from gaining access to a patient portal, but releasing records or changing a caregiver’s access requires a separate authorization decision. Confirming the patient’s identity does not automatically establish that another person should receive their information.

    Benefits administration presents a similar split. Establishing that a claimant exists does not prove eligibility, and verifying eligibility does not authorize every later change. Redirecting a benefit payment should trigger verification tied to that change, using contact details established before the request.

    Across these settings, assurance belongs at the decision where harm becomes possible.

    In a recent development, I would start with the highest-consequence journeys: opening an account, recovering access, changing payment details, releasing sensitive records and moving money. For each, identify the evidence required, the accountable owner and the conditions that should pause execution.

    Layer identity checks deliberately. Document validation, authoritative-source checks, liveness, device signals and behavioral history should contribute different evidence. Five checks derived from the same compromised document do not create five independent reasons for confidence. Liveness detection, which confirms a real, live person is present (rather than a photo, replay or synthetic video), also needs protection against injected media; a live-looking face is insufficient if the capture process itself can be bypassed, for example, by injecting a pre-recorded or AI-generated video directly into the system rather than presenting it to a real camera. NIST’s identity-proofing guidance explicitly addresses forged media and injection attacks.

    Sources indicate that consequential actions require confirmation through a separately established channel. A voice or video call should never, by itself, authorize a payment or sensitive change. Present the actual recipient, amount and action in a trusted application, and require approval bound to those details.

    In a recent development, independence is essential. Calling a number supplied during the suspicious conversation simply returns the organization to the attacker. Account recovery and contact detail changes deserve equivalent scrutiny because they can undermine every later confirmation.

    According to recent reports, even a transaction-specific approval cannot prove that someone understands a scam. Unusual payments may require a cooling-off period, a targeted warning or a conversation with a trained specialist.

    In a recent development, I previously argued that security reviews should follow information through its lifecycle. Fraud assurance needs that perspective too.

    Trace where identity evidence originated, who changed contact details, which device initiated the request and how the destination differs from previous activity. Behavioral signals should inform investigation and proportionate challenges, with privacy limits and a route for legitimate owners to appeal mistakes.

    According to recent reports, govern your own generative AI with equal care. Inventory customer-facing assistants and internal agents, restrict their access and prevent conversational output from becoming authority to change records or release funds. Test whether manipulated inputs can persuade an assistant to bypass verification or expose information useful for impersonation.

    These controls carry costs. Additional checks can delay customers, exclude people with limited documentation and generate false positives. Provide accessible alternatives and measure abandonment and mistaken rejection alongside fraud outcomes.

    As I argued in my ORF America commentary, cybersecurity affects economic security because failures undermine the services and confidence on which commerce depends.

    The fraud metrics reported to the board should lead with realized fraud losses reported both before recoveries and after recoveries, measured against transaction value and broken out by fraud type. Track customer harm, recovery time and legitimate activity blocked alongside them. Detection rates remain diagnostic measures; they are not the outcome. The practical test is whether fewer fraudulent actions succeed, less money is lost and legitimate people can still get things done.​.

Finally, our infrastructure is hosted onshore in Australia and Newly introduced Zealand with reliable and increasingly renewable energy. Each of those advantages matters more as this market matures, and that is the theme of the next few slides. It is worth looking at the market opportunity and why we are building Sharon the way we are.

    According to recent reports, structure Research shows neoclouds like Sharon, which specialize in GPU-based services, gaining a share across every layer of the AI infrastructure. On IT infrastructure, neoclouds made up about 2% of the total IT infrastructure in 2025. However, by 2031, that share is projected to reach over 12%. Within the cloud infrastructure space, the neocloud share is forecasted to roughly triple to about 16% by 2031, while the value of that share, as shown in the middle chart, is forecasted to grow roughly 18x from about $27 billion to over $480 billion. Finally, on AI capacity, neoclouds held about 14% of AI capacity in 2025.

    By 2030, however, that share is projected to reach approximately 33%, while hyperscaler share fall from about 81% to below 60% over the same time period. Put simply, demand for AI compute is growing faster than hyperscalers and the legacy market can build on their own, and growing our share of that capacity is moving to neoclouds. That is the market SharonAI is built to serve. The constraint out there is the ability to deliver this performance-focused infrastructure for the AI age, the power, data center, and GPU capacity all coming together, which is what we are focused on at SharonAI. Our framework for what it takes to win in this market has not changed.

    We think about GPU allocation, power, regulation, and capital and talent. This quarter, I want to spend some time on power, because it is the constraint we hear the most about from customers and investors, and it is where Australia and our model stands apart. In most markets, latest grid connections, substations, and transmission lines carry multi-year lead times. Our model seeks to avoid these by design.

    Every site we deploy into is either an established data center facility that is already connected to the grid, or a new build or the expansion of the existing site where power is already established in that location. Recently, David Burns, our COO, set some of this out in a blog post available on our website. He talked about grid power already being in place, the remaining step to get operational, generally sitting at the data hall level, and where our co-location partners are energizing individual halls. We work with a portfolio of data center providers who are commissioning Tier III and Tier IV data center facilities across multiple sites, so that no single energization determines our overall capacity.

    According to recent reports, what does this translate into? At all of our sites, we know our contracted customers and when power is on site, with no reliance on future grid utility connections or upgrades. This helps us have confidence in our customer delivery dates. In a market where this is constrained, a credible delivery date is a competitive advantage. On other constraints, our NVIDIA partnership continues to support GPU allocation, and we continue to extend our sovereign footprint in Australia. Regarding capital and talent, we have secured approximately $2.6 billion since December last year, and we continue to strengthen our Board and leadership team with high-quality additions. Why Australia? Australia is so well-positioned to capitalize on the global AI infrastructure build-out.

    Global demand for AI compute is outpacing the physical infrastructure needed to deliver it, and timely access to power is increasingly the binding constraint. We believe Australia has the foundation to become a global exporter of AI compute and tokens, and SharonAI is built to take advantage of that. Australia has abundant land, significant energy resources and available power, strong water security, and strong potential for renewable energy at scale. We are close enough to the rest of APAC, but far enough away to be safe and secure. Finally, we have strong connectivity, which ensures low latency delivery as capacity is built out. With this, we are also seeing a change in where compute locates.

    Traditionally, we saw a focus on data center proximity to metro regions, and broadly, cloud computing could be defined by the saying that you bring the power to the compute. AI factories are increasingly characterized by the compute going to the power, however. This shift sees the future AI factories co-located closer to power assets, partly due to this scale requirement, but also due to potential impacts on infrastructure and the local environment. These strategic advantages matter as much to our customers. They know they have a stable government and supportive policy environment, a skilled workforce and world-class research institutions, and strong global connectivity and trusted international relationships, including Australia being part of the Five Eyes alliance.

Australian operational data center capacity is forecast to grow from about 1.6 GW in 2026 to about 3.9 GW by 2030, according to Data Centers Australia. Building AI infrastructure in regional Australia depends on meaningful community engagement and on those local communities sharing the benefits, such as jobs and investment.

It is why we are focused on execution. In doing this, we plan to disclose more component timing for investors to understand where we are operationally.

    Industry observers note that for our global technology customer, for instance, tranche one, which is around 20% of the GPUs in that contract, has been installed and tested, accepted by the customer, and commenced billing in the third quarter.     The Inventory Accuracy Problem Smart Fulfillment Centers Still Need To Solve

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1044 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Amruth Puppala | Senior Engineering Manager | Walmart.
    • In a recent development, ​Walk into a modern fulfillment center, and you will see how much warehouse operations have changed.
    • Yet, even with these advances, a familiar problem remains.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Amruth Puppala | Senior Engineering Manager | Walmart.

    In a recent development, ​Walk into a modern fulfillment center, and you will see how much warehouse operations have changed. Robots move products, software coordinates thousands of orders and inventory systems track merchandise across receiving, storage and shipping.

    Yet, even with these advances, a familiar problem remains.

    A system demonstrates that an item is available, but when someone goes to pick it, the product is not there. The inventory record may be correct on paper, but the physical reality is different. What seems like a minor discrepancy can swiftly turn into additional searches, picking delays, order reallocation or missed shipping commitments.

    According to recent reports, this raises an important question. Instead of simply knowing how much inventory we have, shouldn’t we also know how reliable that information is?

    It has been revealed that fulfillment centers and distribution centers handle enormous volumes of inventory movements every day. Products are received, stored, replenished, picked and shipped, often through a combination of manual processes and automated equipment.

    Even with well-designed systems, discrepancies can occur.

    In a recent development, A pallet may be placed in the wrong location. A receiving transaction might be completed before the merchandise is physically verified. Damaged inventory may not be removed from available stock immediately. Sometimes, a picking exception is recorded without the underlying inventory issue being resolved.

    According to recent reports, warehouses already have processes to investigate these situations. Cycle counting, reconciliation and exception management are essential parts of daily operations.

    However, many discrepancies are discovered only after they begin affecting order fulfillment.

    By that point, the operations team is responding to a problem rather than preventing it.

    One idea worth exploring is assigning a confidence score to inventory records based on the operational evidence supporting them.

    Consider two storage locations, each showing 100 units available. The first location was recently verified, and its last several picking transactions were completed successfully. The second location has experienced repeated picking failures, unexplained quantity adjustments and an unresolved exception.

    Both locations show the same available quantity, but they clearly do not carry the same level of operational confidence.

    It has been revealed that today, many inventory decisions focus primarily on quantity, location and availability. Adding a confidence score could give warehouse systems another useful signal when making those decisions.

    The score would not represent a fresh inventory balance. It would indicate how much confidence the system has in the existing record.

    This could help teams identify which locations need verification and which inventory discrepancies are most likely to affect upcoming orders.

    Recent advances in AI create an opportunity to evaluate these signals continuously rather than relying entirely on scheduled checks.

    A system could monitor receiving transactions, inventory movements, picking results and adjustment history to identify patterns that deserve attention.

    For example, repeated picking failures at the same location might suggest a discrepancy. An unusual sequence of inventory adjustments could indicate a process concern. A location that has not been physically verified for an extended period could warrant additional scrutiny, particularly if the inventory is needed for upcoming shipments.

    Rather than treating each event independently, the system could examine the broader history and determine whether further verification is justified.

    Sources indicate that newer AI models can also help interpret exception notes and other information that traditional rule-based systems may struggle to analyze consistently. Where cameras or robotic sensors are available, their observations could provide additional supporting evidence.

    The key point is that AI should help identify where to investigate, not make inventory adjustments without verification.

    Cycle counting is one area where this approach could have immediate practical value.

    According to recent reports, most distribution centers already use scheduled counting programs, often based on inventory value, product movement or operational requirements. Those methods are useful and should continue.

    However, a fixed schedule does not always account for problems developing during the day.

    It has been revealed that imagine a location that reports 100 units in stock. Several picking attempts fail within a short period, but the inventory quantity remains unchanged. Instead of waiting for the next scheduled count, the system could recommend that the location be checked sooner. The priority could increase if those units are needed for orders approaching their shipping cutoff.

    This would allow inventory teams to focus attention where a potential discrepancy is most likely to cause operational disruption. It could also help avoid unnecessary checks in locations where recent transactions consistently support the recorded inventory.

    I would not recommend introducing another large platform to solve this problem. Most warehouses already generate much of the information needed. The opportunity is to make better use of it.

    A practical starting point would be to combine inventory movement history, picking exceptions, recent count results and upcoming order demand.

    Sources indicate that simple rules could first identify obvious discrepancies. Machine learning could then help recognize less predictable patterns, while newer language models could assist with interpreting operational notes and explaining why a location has been flagged.

    The warehouse management system would remain responsible for inventory records and transactions. Any quantity correction would continue through established verification and approval processes.

    For an initial rollout, I would focus on a limited number of high-volume locations and measure whether the approach reduces repeated picking failures, shortens discrepancy resolution time and improves verification productivity.

    It has been revealed that accuracy matters, but so does the amount of additional work introduced. If the system generates too many unnecessary checks, it has not solved the underlying problem.

    Fulfillment technology has made progress in improving speed, automation and visibility. But visibility alone does not guarantee accuracy.

    A warehouse can have a view of its recorded inventory and still make the wrong fulfillment decision when those records do not match physical conditions.

    The next opportunity is to make inventory reliability a continuous part of warehouse operations, rather than something evaluated through periodic reconciliation.

    According to recent reports, the goal is not to eliminate inventory discrepancies. That would be unrealistic in a continuously operating facility. The goal is to recognize problems earlier, direct people to locations and prevent disruptions before they affect customer orders.

The company is building regulated infrastructure for digital securities, expanding from technology fees into credit origination and trading commissions. With $300 million in liquid balance-sheet reserves, it has significant flexibility to scale institutional partnerships. Three things management stated stand out.

    Management is expanding beyond digital record-keeping into structured asset-backed finance (using real-world collateral, such as loans, to back digital tokens) through its acquisition of the credit platform River One. Moving into origination allows the tech giant to earn net interest margins (the spread between borrowing costs and lending yields) rather than relying solely on fixed servicing fees.

    It has been revealed that tokenized stock offerings require proper legal backing, and Securitize relies on its broker-dealer (a licensed entity that buys and sells securities) licenses rather than temporary regulatory exemptions. Demonstrating compliant equity tokenization with its own stock proves that institutional security entitlement structures can operate inside current U.S. financial rules.

    Large asset managers are bringing investment products on-chain to unlock liquidity and collateral use for institutional clients. Securitize is pursuing fund management fees by partnering with tier-one asset managers across the risk spectrum.

    Sources indicate that revenue expanded 29% sequentially in the third quarter, and management isn't hiding its satisfaction about the underlying operating momentum. Balance sheet liquidity, established transfer-agency capabilities (recording official security ownership), and permanent regulatory licenses position the business to capture shifts in capital market infrastructure. Management is closely monitoring trading-venue execution and tokenized-stock adoption.

    As digital assets gain broader traction among institutional investors, capital deployment across new credit products and public equity venues will determine whether transaction volume becomes the primary driver of growth.

    #50670. Beyond Tokens: Why Intelligence Per Watt Is The Metric That Matters

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1036 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    Beyond Tokens: Why Intelligence Per Watt Is The Metric That Matters

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1036 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Steven Woo, fellow and distinguished inventor at Rambus.
    • In a recent development, ​AI progress centers on tokens: tokens processed, tokens generated, tokens per second and tokens per watt.
    • “Intelligence Per Watt: Measuring Intelligence Efficiency Of Local AI,” published in November 2025 by a Stanford team, found that small local models can accurately answer 88.7% of single-turn chat and reasoning queries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, by Dr. Steven Woo, fellow and distinguished inventor at Rambus.

    In a recent development, ​AI progress centers on tokens: tokens processed, tokens generated, tokens per second and tokens per watt. And because tokens are easy to count, they’ve become the default unit of AI performance. But token-based metrics are only part of the story and miss what consumers really want. A more useful metric, and one closer to the industry’s goal, is how much intelligence a system delivers per watt.​.

    “Intelligence Per Watt: Measuring Intelligence Efficiency Of Local AI,” published in November 2025 by a Stanford team, found that small local models can accurately answer 88.7% of single-turn chat and reasoning queries. Intelligence efficiency—capability delivered per watt—improved 5.3 times between 2023 and 2025, roughly 3.1 times from better models and 1.7 times from better hardware—factors that compound rather than add. This efficiency, not pure token throughput, will determine how well AI can keep scaling.​​.

    Recent findings suggest that ask a CFO, CIO or CTO running AI workloads what worries them, and it’s rarely whether they’re generating enough tokens. Although tokenmaxxing has become a metric that some companies use to measure AI engagement, others see the dangers of simply measuring token consumption independent of productivity and delivered value. Several companies are cutting back on token spending, with Uber among others stating in May 2026 that it had already spent its 2026 AI budget, and their COO adding it was becoming “harder to justify” their internal AI costs. There’s a growing call for valuemaxxing, which directs teams toward measurable outcomes based on the value being generated by these tokens.​.

    It has been revealed that concerns about measuring token usage are compounded by the fact that reasoning models don’t produce a single response per query; they work through an internal chain of intermediate tokens the user never sees. Published work on model development puts these generations in the thousands to tens of thousands of tokens. That means a query can consume far more resources than its visible output suggests.​.

    The pressure to continuously improve value and reduce the cost per token extends beyond inference bills. TrendForce expected server DRAM contract prices to rise 13% to 18% quarter over quarter in Q3 2026, so memory, one of the critical workhorses for AI processing, is getting more expensive as it’s being asked to do more.​​.

    Sources indicate that for hardware companies, that changes the questions being asked. It stops being how many tokens a chip can generate and becomes how much bandwidth memory can deliver per dollar and per watt, and how these metrics will improve in the future.​.

    Sources indicate that for decades, the semiconductor industry relied on Dennard scaling to improve power efficiency. As transistors shrank, they drew less power, so more compute arrived without a matching jump in energy use. That relationship broke down in the mid-2000s as transistors continued to shrink, but the automatic power benefit that used to come with each new process node no longer followed.​.

    It has been revealed that with this lever gone, the industry had to substitute architectural changes for what used to be a by-product of process scaling. Memory is where much of that effort is going: Moving data is a major consumer of system power, making it one of the largest levers to pull.​.

    Sources indicate that the case for stacking DRAM directly on top of a processor has been argued for years. The energy needed to move a bit scales with distance. A DRAM stack beside a processor sits 10 to 12 millimeters away. But stacking the DRAM on top of a processor cuts the distance to about a millimeter. Bandwidth improves separately: Memory beside the processor feeds data through the die’s edges, so interconnect scales with perimeter; stacking can move data through the whole face of a die, allowing bandwidth to scale with area.​.

    Stacking DRAM has become a focus topic of the semiconductor industry. At Hot Chips 2026, Samsung released more details about zHBM, which places the processor beneath the DRAM stack and claims roughly 70% lower I/O power than the previous generation. That’s what more bandwidth per dollar and per watt looks like.​.

    Industry observers note that stacking has manufacturing and engineering challenges. Although silicon conducts heat reasonably well, a stack of DRAM sitting on a hot processor acts like a blanket and prevents heat from being moved away. Samsung’s answer is thinner dies and smaller four-high stacks rather than the 12-high or 16-high configurations conventional HBM supports. The energy saved on data movement is coupled with less thermal resistance to achieve a high performance, thermally viable architecture.​.

    It has been revealed that the same constraint is reshaping infrastructure above the die. Enterprise racks that once drew 20 to 30 kilowatts are heading toward hundreds of kilowatts, and eventually toward a megawatt. Power Electronics Magazine reported in January 2026 that 54 volt in-rack distribution “isn’t designed to support the megawatt-scale racks,” and that the transition to 800 volt DC begins in 2027. Copper is expensive and limits current, so when power demand climbs, voltage is the remaining variable that can rise.​.

    Delivering the most intelligence for a given dollar and a given watt used to be determined by two scaling trends running together: Moore’s law delivered more transistors per dollar, and Dennard scaling delivered them at lower power. Moore’s law continues, albeit at a slower pace. Dennard scaling doesn’t, so the power portion of that result now has to be engineered deliberately, architecture by architecture.​.

    The industry has hit walls like this before, and the solution was rarely a single breakthrough. It was a return to fundamentals: measuring the right thing and re-architecting around the real constraint instead of the metric that’s easiest to report.​.

    In a recent development, for the CFOs, CIOs and CTOs approving AI budgets, and for the hardware and software teams underneath them, the number worth tracking isn’t simply how many tokens a system produces. It’s how much usable intelligence and value these tokens return for the dollars and the watts spent producing them.

    • Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.
    • It has been revealed that here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept.
    • Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

    It has been revealed that here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

    Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

    Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

    In a recent development, robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly vital sources of transaction revenue, while the firm has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

    Industry observers note that transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

    Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

    Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

    Recent findings suggest that net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

    —With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney.

    #50657. As Power Demand Surges, Energy Is Moving Closer To The Edge

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (885 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

    As Power Demand Surges, Energy Is Moving Closer To The Edge

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (885 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • ​Over the summer, Europe suffered a heat wave that strained its power grids, simultaneously increasing electricity demand and forcing some power plants to shut down.​.
    • This isn’t the first time extreme temperatures have impacted the grid’s ability to deliver power.
    • Sources indicate that the problem is being made worse by the construction of hyperscale AI data centers, which require massive amounts of electricity and further strain the grid.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Darren H. S. Tan. Chief Executive Officer at UNIGRID.

    ​Over the summer, Europe suffered a heat wave that strained its power grids, simultaneously increasing electricity demand and forcing some power plants to shut down.​.

    This isn’t the first time extreme temperatures have impacted the grid’s ability to deliver power. Many places around the world have experienced record-high or record-low temperatures in recent years, and the demand for heating or cooling reached levels that existing energy infrastructure wasn’t designed to handle. ​.

    Sources indicate that the problem is being made worse by the construction of hyperscale AI data centers, which require massive amounts of electricity and further strain the grid. Completely rebuilding the grid to meet modern demands has proven fiscally impractical for many governments, forcing many places to solve the problem on the local level using distributed generation and storage.

    Sources indicate that energy infrastructure across the U.S. and Europe was built over a century ago, when energy needs were much different. ​.

    Even so, studies have shown that we use only about 40% to 55% of the grid on average, and that’s by design, so it can handle spikes when they occur. But recent extreme weather events and data center demand are causing power needs to exceed even that generous buffer.​.

    For example, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), which manages electricity in Texas, has mentioned its interconnection queue right now includes over 1,800 projects totaling 474 gigawatts of power, over five times the state’s record peak electricity demand. Ninety percent of those requests come from data centers. ​.

    The cost to completely rebuild the grid to meet today’s needs is astronomical, with some estimates putting the total replacement cost in the trillions. Because of the potential cost and the fact that the aging grid is a chronic rather than an urgent problem, it receives patchwork upgrades as needed and as government budgets allow. ​.

    With a full rebuild out of the picture, several strategies are in play to work within the system we already have. When demand approaches available supply, energy companies offer rebates for reducing usage at peak times, implement peak pricing or, in more extreme cases, resort to rolling blackouts, which are planned outages to alleviate the demand during peak periods. ​.

    Beyond the grid itself, some areas are reducing their dependence on the centralized infrastructure by moving toward local power generation and storage.

    Industry observers note that battery energy storage systems (BESS) can store electricity and discharge it when demand exceeds the grid’s capacity. ​.

    It has been revealed that they are already showing promise in several states, such as California, where battery storage capacity has reached over 21,000 MW, equal to about one-third of the state’s peak demand. Eighty percent of that capacity is represented by grid-connected batteries, but smaller batteries are also enabling residents to increase their own energy storage capacity at home.​.

    In a recent development, as these batteries become cheaper and more reliable, it’s not out of the realm of possibility that these energy storage systems become a standard household appliance in the future, much like a refrigerator or washing machine is today. They can also play a role in energy needs for small businesses.

    In a recent development, being able to store energy and use it in an emergency is only half the equation. The other half is being able to generate electricity independently of the grid. ​.

    According to recent reports, this isn’t a concept that should be unfamiliar to many, as many organizations and homes already have backup generators or solar panels. Although these methods can keep small businesses and homes powered up, they have their disadvantages. Generators are noisy, pollutive and can be dangerous, while solar has significant upfront installation costs. ​.

    In a recent development, plug-in solar is emerging as another option for generating electricity locally that has already seen success in Europe and is starting to gain support in the U.S. as well. Instead of being installed on a rooftop, these smaller panels can be mounted on a balcony or a small section of a yard or business property and plugged into a wall outlet to help power homes and small businesses. ​.

    In a recent development, these systems cost significantly less than traditional solar and are portable, so people can move them around wherever they’re needed. These benefits open up power generation to a whole new segment of the country: commercial and residential renters alike who might never invest in a hardwired battery system or solar installation.

    As energy demand continues to increase, expanding traditional grid infrastructure will remain important, but those projects can be expensive and take years to complete. Distributed generation and storage offer another way to increase resilience in the meantime. ​.

    By generating and storing more electricity closer to where it will be consumed, communities and business leaders can help reduce their reliance on the centralized grid during peak demand.​.

    We’re unlikely to solve growing power constraints with any single technology, but as local generation and storage become cheaper and more accessible, they can play a larger role in managing peak demand and making better use of the grid infrastructure we already have.​.

    10 stocks we like better than Jumia Technologies Ag ›.

    On its third quarter of 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 18, 2026, Jumia (JMIA -8.76%) declared that its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) loss narrowed 43% year over year to $7.9 million. The e-commerce operator is proving its monetization strategy can shrink losses even as high memory chip costs hurt smartphone supply across Africa. Long-term gains depend on whether management can reignite customer growth without burning cash.

    Three takeaways from the call reveal where the business is headed.

    Recent findings suggest that global memory chip price spikes have driven up prices and caused shortages for smartphones and other electronics across key markets. Smartphones serve as the main gateway for newly introduced shoppers; hardware price inflation is dampening broader engagement.

    Jumia is increasing its gross margins by cutting costs and improving monetization. Management isn't buying top-line growth through heavy promotional discounts. Instead, higher commission rates and expanding retail advertising services are pushing gross margins higher while keeping fixed overhead lean.

    In a recent development, external factors, including smartphone supply and cocoa prices, have put pressure on customers. Jumia's management believes its value offering will help it gain market share. The strategy relies on removing user friction and improving software conversion tools rather than increasing marketing spend.

    It has been revealed that jumia updated its full-year 2026 guidance because its early Black Friday trends were below expectations, particularly in the Ivory Coast. Management is using headcount reductions and artificial intelligence tools to trim operational expenses. It is improving its pickup station logistics network, expanding international merchant sourcing, and maintaining strict fee discipline to protect unit margins.

    If logistics expansion and social affiliate tools reignite order volume, the enterprise can compound value on a leaner overhead structure.

    How Damian Lillard has boosted Trail Blazers in promising return from Achilles injury

    💡 Key Takeaways
